facts.text: UN R131 and UN R152 allow the driver to interrupt warnings and emergency braking through a conscious action such as accelerator kick-down or swerving.

facts.text: On-road braking logic delays braking until the last possible moment to reduce false positives.

facts.text: AAA test protocols from 2024 monitor brake-pedal force to confirm whether the driver applied the brakes.

facts.text: On-road logic described in US patent 11427166 delays braking until steering avoidance is no longer possible, or brakes earlier when steering avoidance is blocked.
facts.quote: Some logic delays braking until steering avoidance is no longer possible, or brakes earlier when steering avoidance is blocked (US patent 11427166).

facts.text: ISO 21815-3 requires a collision-avoidance system not to override operator braking when the operator's braking exceeds the system's braking demand.
facts.quote: the collision-avoidance system must not override operator braking when the operator's braking is greater than the system's braking demand

facts.text: ISO 21815-3 permits intentional operator control to override an automatic intervention where appropriate.
facts.quote: intentional operator control may be permitted to override an automatic intervention where appropriate.

facts.text: The Hitachi mining-truck patent checks brake-pedal stroke after the second alarm to determine that an avoidance action has been performed.

facts.text: The Hitachi mining-truck patent switches off the first alarm once time to collision recovers above the first limit.

facts.text: University of Pretoria work from 2024 samples plausible Gaussian steering-rate trajectories to predict collisions and reduce false brake interventions on mining vehicles; the reported initial results are simulation-only.

facts.text: No off-road validation was found for the recommended fusion of operator and machine signals to recognize that the operator is already reacting.
facts.quote: **Signals a production system should fuse** (**Expert opinion**; no off-road validation found)

facts.text: A production collision-mitigation system should fuse brake pedal or lever demand, brake pressure, and requested brake torque as direct braking cues, crediting actual achieved or predicted deceleration rather than switch status.
facts.quote: | Brake pedal or lever demand, brake pressure, requested brake torque | Direct braking action | Credit according to actual achieved or predicted deceleration, not switch status |

facts.text: A production collision-mitigation system should treat a hydrostatic swashplate, propel lever, or travel lever moving toward neutral as a slowing request, but credit the request only if the machine is actually losing speed fast enough.
facts.quote: | Hydrostatic swashplate, propel or travel lever returned toward neutral | Operator requesting slowing | Credit only if the machine is actually losing speed fast enough |

facts.text: A production collision-mitigation system should treat retarder or inching-pedal requests as active deceleration cues and include measured retarder response and delay.
facts.quote: | Retarder or inching pedal request | Active deceleration | Include the measured retarder response and delay |

facts.text: A production collision-mitigation system should use steering or articulation command and rate as possible evasive-path cues, suppressing braking only when predicted collision risk is demonstrably falling; steering alone is not proof of safety.
facts.quote: | Steering or articulation command and rate | Possible evasive path change | Suppress braking only if predicted collision risk is demonstrably falling; steering alone is not proof of safety |

facts.text: Releasing accelerator or propel demand is weak evidence of an early operator reaction because a downhill machine can accelerate after throttle release.
facts.quote: | Accelerator or propel demand released | Early reaction | Weak evidence; a downhill machine can accelerate after throttle release |

facts.text: A production collision-mitigation system should treat direction-lever changes or reversal requests as potential avoidance cues while accounting for hydrostatic or transmission delay and the danger of a new collision in the opposite direction.
facts.quote: | Direction-lever change or reversal request | Potential avoidance | Account for hydrostatic or transmission delay and the danger of a new collision in the opposite direction |

facts.text: Measured longitudinal deceleration is a strong physical confirmation of operator response, but is delayed relative to operator intent.
facts.quote: | Measured longitudinal deceleration | Physical confirmation of response | Strong signal, but delayed relative to intent |

facts.text: A predicted path moving away from an object indicates effective avoidance and provides a strong cross-check for steering or articulation responses.
facts.quote: | Predicted path moving away from the object | Avoidance becoming effective | Strong cross-check for steering or articulation responses |

facts.text: Measured deceleration is the most physically meaningful braking cue; automatic intervention should be suppressed if a_measured ≥ a_required plus a margin.
facts.quote: The last of the braking cues is the most physically meaningful: if a_measured ≥ a_required plus a margin, suppress the intervention.

facts.text: Automatic intervention should not be suppressed merely because an operator control moved; suppression or reduction should require the operator's action to produce a collision-avoidance trajectory at least as safe as the automatic action.
facts.quote: do not suppress automatic intervention merely because an operator control moved; suppress or reduce it when the operator's action produces a collision-avoidance trajectory at least as safe as the automatic action.

facts.text: A common failure occurs when a startled operator briefly releases the accelerator or touches the brake, causing the automatic system to stand down while the remaining stopping margin continues collapsing.
facts.quote: a common failure in which a startled operator briefly releases the accelerator or touches the brake, the automatic system stands down, and the remaining stopping margin keeps collapsing.

facts.text: After an automatic stop, the control state should use hysteresis and an explicit release condition; this expert recommendation is anchored in ISO 21815-3's rollaway provision.
facts.quote: After an automatic stop, the control state should use hysteresis and an explicit release condition

facts.text: On slopes, collision-system braking should not be released merely because the detected object disappears for one sensor frame; this expert recommendation is anchored in ISO 21815-3's rollaway provision.
facts.quote: on slopes, do not release collision-system braking because the detected object disappears for one sensor frame.
